sources.quote: The name "baryon", introduced by Abraham Pais, comes from the Greek word for "heavy" (βαρύς, barýs), because, at the time of their naming, most known elementary particles had lower masses than the baryons.

The muon is an elementary particle..why: Stated in the first sentence of every description of the muon: it is an elementary particle, a heavier cousin of the electron. It is written as a sentence of its own, not worked out from 'lepton'.

notes: Dev-split ABox revision (all determinate, no worlds): the muon changes class (in_particle_family: lepton to baryon), so the class rules of baryons reach it. The one related question asks whether the muon is an elementary particle (stored; a baryon not made of quarks is not allowed by any world, so the answer overturns). Derived: the meaning of the Greek root of the family name (composition through a fact about baryons), the chain to hadron, and the baryon number of a beam of 1,000 muons (inheritance, application with arithmetic). in_particle_family is tagged subproperty:instance_of and functional (the particle families partition the particles). Direct and paraphrase name their two options (lepton or baryon), because an open "which family" invites the right but useless answer "fermion". The bridge "every baryon is made of three quarks" is avoided because pentaquarks are baryons too; baryon number 1 holds for every baryon. The near unrelated question asks the tau's family (lepton), catching an edit that spreads to leptons in general.
